Introduction to Counterpoint: Practice for Chapter 30

Chapter 30 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: first and second species counterpoint in two voices over a cantus firmus, with checked examples and exercises, and a map of the rest of the chapter (third to fifth species, invention expositions, fugue analysis).

This page goes with Chapter 30, Introduction to Counterpoint of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. It builds on Voice Leading Triads (the types of motion and the rules of melody in 26.1 and 26.4).

How the page works. Each example is drawn on a grand staff, plays when you press Play, and is marked by the same checker that marks your exercises: a green Right passes it, a red Wrong shows what the checker says. In the exercises the given notes are greyed; type the others (E4, F#4, Bb3; Up and Down move a step in the key, Shift a half step) and press Check.

Every counterpoint is written in two voices against a given cantus firmus (c.f.), a plain melody in whole notes. Here the cantus firmus is in the lower voice (counterpoint above) or in the upper voice (counterpoint below); the page says which.

30.1 Species counterpoint

Fux’s Gradus ad Parnassum (1725) teaches writing by species: one, two, three or four notes against each whole note of the cantus firmus, in the style of Palestrina. Counterpoint is the sounding together of melodic lines (a contrapuntal texture), in contrast to melody and accompaniment (homophonic). The book’s rules are a simplified version of Fux’s; the page’s checker marks all five species. The invention and fugue sections at the end are described, not checked.

30.2 First species: note against note

Write one whole note for each note of the cantus firmus. The rules (simplified from Fux, as in the book):

  • Begin and end on a unison or octave. Approach the final octave by contrary motion: one voice 7 to 8 (a half step up, with a raised leading tone in G mixolydian, D dorian and A aeolian), the other 2 to 1.
  • Every interval is a consonance: unison, 3rd, 5th, 6th, octave and their compounds. 2nds, 4ths, 7ths and the tritone are dissonant and not allowed in first species.
  • Imperfect consonances (3rds, 6ths) may be approached any way; perfect consonances (unison, 5th, octave) only by contrary motion, to avoid direct fifths and octaves.
  • Not more than three 3rds (or 6ths) in a row.
  • When the cantus firmus is in the upper part, the counterpoint below uses unison, 3rd, 5th or 6th.
  • Only these leaps: 3rds, 4ths, 5ths, ascending minor 6ths, octaves; after a leap larger than a 4th, change direction. Do not outline a tritone with two turning points. Avoid repeated notes (they hold up the flow).
The cantus firmus in the bass, a counterpoint above it: octave to start, 3rds and 6ths, the octave on the fourth note approached in contrary motion, 7 to 8 against 2 to 1 at the end.
It begins on a fifth (A above D).
Bar 6: B above F is a tritone, a dissonance.
Bar 4: the fifth A over D is reached in similar motion (both voices fall): a direct fifth.
Bar 6: the leap of a major sixth (B up to G#) is not in the list of leaps.
Bars 5 to 8 are four 3rds in a row.
The ending: F falls to D while the cantus firmus falls E to D: similar motion into the octave.

Exercises: first species

One. Cantus firmus below (D dorian). Write the counterpoint above it. Begin on the octave: D4. In the last bars: C#4 then D4.

Two. Cantus firmus above (D dorian). The counterpoint is below: begin on the octave, D4. A 3rd, 5th or 6th below the cantus firmus is consonant.

30.3 Second species: two against one

Write two half notes against each whole note of the cantus firmus. (In 3/2, three half notes against a dotted whole.) The rules are the same on the downbeats, with these changes:

  • Begin with a half note at the octave or unison on beat 1, or on beat 3 after a half rest.
  • End with a whole note on the octave or unison. The bar before: with the cantus firmus below, a 5th then a 6th above it (6 7 against the cantus firmus’s 2); with it above, a 5th then a 3rd below it. (Phrygian, cantus firmus above: a 6th then a 3rd.)
  • The first half note of a bar is always a consonance. The second is a consonance, or a dissonance only as a passing tone (reached and left by step in the same direction).
  • Across the barline, imperfect consonances are free, perfect ones only by contrary motion. Do not repeat a note across a barline. Avoid octaves on consecutive downbeats, and fifths on consecutive downbeats, unless a leap of a 4th follows the first.
A four-bar example: half rest then D (octave), a bar of 3rd and unison, the 5th to 6th before the end, the final octave.
Bar 2: the A over G is a dissonant second half note that is left by a leap, not a passing tone.
Bar 2 ends on B and bar 3 begins on B: a repeated note across the barline.
The bar before the end is a 3rd and a 5th, not the 5th and 6th the ending needs.

Exercise: second species

Cantus firmus below (D dorian). Begin with a half rest and a half note D4 (leave the first box of bar 1 empty). Bar 5 is the bar before the end: a fifth and a sixth above E3. The last bar is one box.

30.4 Third species: four against one

Write four quarter notes to each whole note of the cantus firmus (the last bar one whole note). Begin on an octave or unison. The rules of first species still hold on the downbeats, plus:

  • Each downbeat is a consonance. The other three quarters may be consonant, or dissonant only as a passing tone (never on beat 1) or the cambiata: approached by a step down from beat 1 to beat 2, left by a leap down a third, then a step up.
  • Across the barline, imperfect consonances are free; a perfect one on the downbeat only by contrary motion (no direct fifths or octaves). Do not repeat a note across a barline.
  • The ending: a whole note on an octave or unison. The bar before it, in scale degrees: with the cantus firmus below, 4 5 6 7 or the cambiata 2 1 6 7; with the cantus firmus above, 7 5 6 7. The note before the end rises a half step.
The cantus firmus in the bass (D F E D): the downbeats are consonant, G passes between A and F, and the bar before the end is 4 5 6 7 (G A B C#) over E.
Bar 2 starts on G over F: a dissonant downbeat.
Bar 1: the E over D is dissonant and is left by a leap, so it is not a passing tone.
The bar before the end is 4 6 5 7, not 4 5 6 7.
Bar 1 ends on F and bar 2 starts on F: a repeated note across the barline.

Exercise: third species

Cantus firmus below (D dorian). Begin on D4, end D5 (one note); in the bar before the end write G4 A4 B4 C#5. Four boxes a bar.

30.5 Fourth species: suspensions

Here the counterpoint is syncopated: the book writes fourth species only with the cantus firmus in the lower voice.

  • Start with a half rest, then a half note an octave above the cantus firmus. End with a whole note an octave above it.
  • The half note on beat 3 of every bar except the penultimate is tied across the barline to the first half note of the next bar. Beat 3 is always a consonance.
  • If the tied note, on the next downbeat, is a dissonance (a 4th or a 7th above the cantus firmus) it is a suspension and must resolve down by step. Allowed in the upper part: 4-3 and 7-6; 9-8 and 2-1 are not allowed. If the tied note is a consonance it is a syncopation and may go anywhere.
  • The penultimate bar has a 7-6 suspension (over the cantus firmus’s 2, a 7th resolving to the 6th, then up to the final octave).
Half rest, D an octave above, then ties: D over G (a syncopation), E over F (a 7th, a suspension resolving to D), and D over E (the 7-6 that closes).
Bar 3: the suspended E (a 7th over F) rises to F instead of falling to D.
Bar 3 does not begin with the E tied over from bar 2.
The bar before the end has no 7-6 suspension.

Exercise: fourth species

Cantus firmus below (D dorian). Leave the first box of bar 1 empty (the half rest) and write D4 in the second. The second box of one bar and the first of the next are the same note, tied.

30.6 Fifth species: florid counterpoint

Fifth species is a free mixture of the first four: half notes, quarter notes and ties in one line over the cantus firmus. Hutchinson points to the opening of Lassus’s Expectatio Justorum as an example. The checker uses what the species above establish: the first and last rules; consonant downbeats, or a tied suspension resolving down by step; dissonance only on a quarter note, as a passing tone, a neighbor tone or a cambiata; perfect consonances on non-tied downbeats only by contrary motion; the allowed leaps. (The neighbor tone as a dissonance and the quarter-note limit are this site’s reading of “a free mixture”, not rules the book states.) Type each bar as notes with lengths, D4:2 E4:1 D4:1 (:2 half, :1 quarter, r:2 a half rest); a note with no length is the bar divided evenly.

Half rest and D, then a half note A with a passing G to F, then G B C# up to the final D.
A tied E (a 7th over F) is suspended, resolves to D, and the D is tied into the closing 7-6.
Bar 2: a half-note G over F is a dissonance that lasts too long.

Exercise: fifth species

Cantus firmus below (D dorian). Try quarter notes and a tie: bar 1 r:2 D4:2; bar 6 one note.

30.7 Invention expositions and fugue analysis

The chapter ends with applying species to harmony: writing the four-bar exposition of a two-part invention on the model of Bach’s C major and E minor inventions (the theme in bar 1, an octave lower in the bass in bar 2, a fifth higher in bar 3, an octave lower in bar 4, ending on a tenth: tonic in the bass, 3 above), with counterpoint that outlines the harmony of each bar (I, then V, then back to I); and analysing a fugue: subject, answer (real or tonal), countersubject, episode, bridge and exposition, with motivic fragmentation. Open the Bach fugue and invention scores in the Analysed Scores Library to hear and see them. Not checked here.

NoteWhat the checker does and does not check
  • First species: beginning, ending (contrary, 7 to 8 and 2 to 1), consonance, perfect intervals only by contrary motion, runs of 3rds and 6ths (this site reads it as three of the same kind), allowed leaps, direction change after leaps larger than a 4th, outlined tritones, repeated notes (a warning).
  • Second species: the beginning on beat 1 or 3, the whole-note ending, the penultimate-bar formulas, consonant downbeats, dissonant second notes only as passing tones, no repeated note across the barline, no octaves or fifths on consecutive downbeats unless a 4th leap follows.
  • Third species: consonant downbeats, passing tones and the cambiata, the 4 5 6 7 / 2 1 6 7 / 7 5 6 7 ending formulas, no repeated note across a barline. Fourth: the tie on every beat 3 but the penultimate, suspensions 4-3 and 7-6 resolving down by step (9-8 and 2-1 refused), the 7-6 before the end. Fifth: the common rules plus the quarter-note limit on dissonance (this site’s reading of “a free mixture”).
  • All species: the counterpoint stays above (or below) the cantus firmus, and the note before the end rises a half step (the book gives this as 7 to 8; the checker requires it in every species, so a Phrygian cantus firmus is allowed a whole step).
  • Not checked: consecutive leaps outlining a triad in species, the range of the counterpoint, fourth species with the cantus firmus above (the book does not write it), and the invention and fugue sections.
